Your heroes are not expendable. They have names. They have friends. They have lovers. They have opinions about their equipment. And when they die—permanently—your guild will never quite be the same.

Hero's Guild is a guild management roguelike. Recruit heroes from the tavern, train them, argue with them about party composition, send them into dungeons that are actively trying to kill them, and watch as their lives become a story you didn't write and can't entirely control. The heroes have their own feelings about everything. They are not always helpful feelings.

HEROES WHO ARE, UNFORTUNATELY, PEOPLE


Every hero arrives with a personality. Not a stat page pretending to be a personality—an actual disposition that determines whether they'll make friends, start fights, fall in love with the worst possible candidate, or quietly hold a grudge for forty in-game days before exploding at a dinner party.

Relationships develop across many tiers, from outright hostility to the kind of devotion that produces either legendary teamwork or catastrophic grief when something goes wrong. Heroes argue. They reconcile. They fall in love, get married at your chapel, and name their swords after each other. Or they develop a blood feud that makes party composition a diplomatic negotiation.

When mood breaks, so do heroes. Push them too hard and they'll desert, go berserk, confess secrets that unravel friendships, or simply take a personal day at the worst possible time. The tavern offers drinks, feasts, gambling nights, and a bard—all valid therapeutic approaches. None of them guaranteed.

THEY WANT THINGS, AND THEY DON'T TELL YOU


Every hero is quietly saving for something. A better cloak. A small house. A name that outlasts them. They never mention it, and they go on wanting it whether or not you ever notice.

They also hold convictions—about mercy, about money, about whether loyalty is a virtue or a tactical error—and those convictions drift according to what you actually make them do. Order a party to leave a wounded stranger in a crypt and they will remember it. Not as a debuff. As a change of mind.

YOU COMMAND. YOU DO NOT PUPPET.


Combat is turn-based, and it resolves itself in front of you. Heroes pick their own targets and their own spells according to the tactics you set—Reckless, Aggressive, Balanced, Cautious, Survival—and according to who they happen to be fighting beside, and whether they can stand them.

Your job is to intervene. Pause whenever you like. Run it at single, double or quadruple speed. Change the tactical preset mid-fight, once it becomes clear that Balanced was an act of optimism. And spend command points—a small budget, refreshed each floor, never quite enough—on a battle cry, a shield wall, an emergency heal, a cleanse, a guaranteed round of crits, or the order to leave right now with whatever you're still holding.

That last one is the most important button in the game, and by far the hardest to press.

Or hand the expedition over entirely and let it run unsupervised while you deal with the guild. Nobody will intervene on your heroes' behalf. Events will proceed regardless.

PERMADEATH THAT MEANS SOMETHING


Death is permanent. But it isn't random, and it is never meaningless.

When a hero falls, their friends grieve. Lovers may never recover. After three days, you hold a burial ceremony. Their name joins the memorial. The guild carries on, slightly emptier.

But heroes protect the people they care about. Send close friends into battle and they may intervene—stepping between a companion and a killing blow. Devoted lovers will sacrifice themselves without being asked. The relationships you build are not decorative. They are the difference between a hero coming home and a hero becoming a plaque.

THE BODY REMEMBERS


Combat leaves marks. Heroes have individual body parts—eyes, arms, legs, organs—and each one can be damaged, destroyed, and eventually replaced. A shattered arm reduces effectiveness. A destroyed eye impairs accuracy. A wounded leg means your fastest rogue now arrives second.

Three tiers of prosthetics offer escalating solutions. A peg leg gets someone walking. A mechanical arm restores function. An enchanted replacement exceeds the original—though the hero wearing it will remain cross about the troll that necessitated it.

Heroes also fall ill. Some illnesses pass. Some leave something chronic behind, which the hero then carries for the rest of a career that is now measurably shorter. The infirmary treats, the ward isolates, and the plague that arrives the week before a raid is not a scripted event—it simply arrived.

And some of them drink. The tavern is therapy until it stops being therapy, at which point there is a detox ward, a long unpleasant fortnight, and a hero who may or may not thank you.

A PASSIVE TREE THE SIZE OF YOUR AMBITION


Six classes. One enormous hexagonal passive tree connecting all of them. Each hero starts at their class node and works outward, spending a point every level. By endgame they'll have invested in roughly a quarter of what's available—enough to feel dangerously specialized, never enough to feel safe.

Minor nodes, major notables, and keystones that fundamentally change how a hero operates—at a cost, because every keystone has a drawback and the tree has opinions about balance. Cross-class bridges let your Warrior pick up spell damage if you'll spend the routing points. Respec is free. Experimentation is encouraged. Regret is also free.

ASCENDANCY: CHOOSE WHAT YOU BECOME


At level 25, each hero faces a solo tower trial. Survive, and they choose an ascendancy—a specialization that reshapes their role entirely. Fourteen paths across six classes, from the Champion (a Warrior who has concluded that not dying is a viable combat strategy) to the Puppeteer (a Necromancer who believes delegation should include the dead).

Four trials. Four points. Ten nodes per path, of which you will ever fill four. Permanent enough to matter, reversible enough not to panic about.

DUNGEONS WITH DECISIONS


Seven environments. Forests where the ambushes come in threes. Crypts where the Cleric's specialized training finally justifies the recruitment cost. Volcanoes where fire resistance was obvious and somebody still forgot. Fog of war keeps the map dark until you're already committed.

Moral events live inside dungeons. A wounded traveler. A sealed coffin. An imprisoned mage whose eyes could be grateful or murderous. Each offers choices with immediate and lasting consequences. Some only fire when a particular hero is present—the right trait, the wrong mood, a specific bond. The dungeon pays attention to who you brought.

Environmental hazards test composition. Toxic gas wants a Cleric. A collapsing ceiling wants a Ranger. Bring the right class and the problem resolves quietly. Bring the wrong party and everyone bleeds through anyway, slightly poorer and measurably less healthy.

ENDGAME: THE CEILING KEEPS GOING UP


Heroic Dungeons — Weekly rotating challenges with modifiers that demand specific builds. Entry-level content for guilds that have stopped being entry-level.

World Bosses — Raid bosses fought by several parties at once, with telegraphed mechanics you are expected to answer rather than survive by accident. The Ancient Dragon, the Skeletal Lich and the Void Titan have no interest whatsoever in your relationship chart, which is the only mercy any of them offers.

The Abyssal Spire — An endless tower where enemies start at level 100 and climb from there. Four heroes. No permadeath, but a leaderboard that remembers exactly how far you got, and therefore where you failed. The Spire doesn't end. You do.

Quest Chains — Story campaigns, class-specific arcs, and weekly bounties, with finale rewards that include named legendary items and—in two cases—a hero who simply turns up and joins, pre-equipped and opinionated.

Prestige Missions — World threats, legendary hunts, and contracts that pay extraordinarily well because somebody has to fight the Elder Dragon and it is plainly not going to be the people offering the contract.

Custom Dungeons (beta) — Build your own dungeons, place the enemies and the traps yourself, and share them with other guilds. In beta, which here means it works and is still being argued with.

THE GUILD IS A CHARACTER


Your guild develops a moral identity across three axes—Valor, Wealth and Order—tracked with the quiet persistence of a very thorough accountant. Every significant decision nudges them. A guild that hoards gold attracts merchants and their temptations. A guild fixated on order eventually meets a problem that order alone cannot solve.

Nightly tavern events demand your attention, literally. Limited attention points, too many situations, and the ones you ignore tonight will be waiting tomorrow, slightly worse. Heroes are in conflict. Someone needs encouragement. A romance is either starting or ending, depending on the next five minutes.

Context-aware events scan your roster continuously. A rivalry at boiling point. A veteran gone unacknowledged. A near-death hero reconsidering their career. They use their names. They have deadlines. Ignore them and the game resolves it for you, defaulting to the least interesting option available.

CHRONICLES: EVERY HERO WRITES THEIR OWN STORY


Each hero keeps a chronicle—a running autobiography assembled from their achievements, their relationships, the dungeons they survived, the friends they lost and the tavern decisions they'd rather not discuss. It writes itself. It reads like a life. By endgame it is a complete narrative that nobody scripted.

Heroes who live long enough retire, which is its own kind of ending, and the guild throws them a party whether or not it can afford one.

EQUIPMENT WITH OPINIONS


Heroes develop attachment to their gear—from merely Comfortable to genuinely Soulbound. Unequip a soulbound weapon and watch their mood crater with the quiet devastation of someone who has been personally betrayed.

Famous forges craft equipment with distinct styles. Heroes develop brand loyalty. And boycotts.

"Thalia refuses to wear Grimforge armor. Says it's 'unethical.' Meanwhile, Garrett won't touch anything that isn't Kothric-made—calls everything else 'flimsy elf-craft.'"

Forge scandals break. Loyal customers suffer. Rival-brand enthusiasts feel vindicated. The economy has feelings. The feelings have consequences.

BUILD YOUR GUILD


Facilities to construct and upgrade. A tavern for recruitment and morale. Forges, workshops and alchemy labs for crafting. A chapel for blessings and burials. An infirmary for before the chapel is needed. Hero quarters with adjacency bonuses, because where your heroes sleep affects how they wake up.

A materials market with dynamic pricing, because even dungeon loot has to be traded for something useful eventually.

Rise through guild ranks to unlock expedition slots, better recruits, and the kind of mission that requires a very specific answer to "are you sure?"

THE ROSTER PUZZLE


You're not a god moving chess pieces. You're a guild master herding cats—brilliant, deadly, emotionally unstable cats who sometimes fall in love with each other and sometimes try to kill each other.

"I had to send Aldric and Theron together even though they hate each other, because Elena refused to go back to the Crypt (her brother died there), Marcus was hungover, and Sofia took a personal day. It was a disaster—they fought the whole time—but they made it. Barely. Now Theron has 'grudging respect.' Aldric still hates him. "

"My best ranger lost her arm to a troll. Took three weeks to craft a prosthetic, but now she's got an enchanted arm that's actually BETTER than the original. She's still bitter about the troll though."

This isn't a bug. This is the game.

INSPIRED BY THE BEST


If you love the psychological tension of Darkest Dungeon, the emergent relationships of RimWorld, the deep build-crafting of Path of Exile and the strategic management of Guild of Dungeoneering—Hero's Guild combines those inspirations into something that frequently surprises even the person running it.

Your guild awaits. Your heroes await. Their drama—extensive, personal and largely unauthorized—also awaits.

Explore a Fantasy World



The game will ultimately feature 9 major races, 60+ creature types, 20+ heroes, and 40+ spells. Choose your hero commander, recruit units ranging from the cavalry of the Sacred Castle to the Bone Dragons of the Undead Necropolis, and build your own armies.

Build Your Army


Start with a single hero, explore events and resource points across the battlefield, manage your resources wisely, recruit units, and combine them to form a powerful army.

Battlefield Upgrade


Analyze the battlefield, choose the right upgrades, and develop a unique army.

Training Records



Build a powerful army during Training and carry its lineup and upgrade effects into special game modes. Face greater threats—or challenge other players head-on.

Build Your Empire




Recruit and train your troops, forge treasures, research magic, upgrade production buildings, and build a mighty empire.

Collect Treasures



Collect all kinds of treasures, equip your army, combine affix effects freely, and build more diverse and powerful armies.

Magic



Earth, Water, Fire, and Air—collect all kinds of spells, from the most basic Magic Arrow to Armageddon. Each hero can equip multiple spells and turn the tide of battle at critical moments.

Multiplayer Modes




Deploy the army you've carefully built in the Arena and battle other players. Who will come out on top?

More to Come

Survival challenges? Co-op mode? More single-player and multiplayer modes are in development!

​Heroes of Aetheria: Crystal Siege

You were born with a hexagonal mark on your back.

People called its power a gift from the gods. The kingdom called it a threat, and kept you on the farthest frontier for ten years.

The day you returned, four legions had poured through a gate torn open in the eastern sky. The capital, and the village you once called home, were already ash.

No one ever told you why this power was given, or what it takes in return. For the first time, the path is yours to draw.

Hexborne is a dark fantasy roguelite RPG where you fight by drawing single-stroke paths across a hex grid.

◆ One stroke at a time

Draw one unbroken path. Every tile you cross counts: sword tiles become attack, shield tiles armor, healing tiles health, and coins gold. Mix them freely in a single path and decide what this turn needs most.

◆ Your path is your swordplay

How your path meets an enemy decides the strike. Leap onto the first foe and plunge down, charge in a straight line to send them flying, circle close and spin through them, cut clean through the ranks, or slash in from the flank. Knocked-back enemies crash into walls, into each other, and onto fire and spikes. The whole battlefield is your weapon.

◆ Grow your Sword Arts, uncover the Chains

Begin with one of five starting Sword Arts. Each level-up can teach you a new art or hone one you know, up to rank 7. Land different strikes at different points of the same path to etch a hidden Sword Chain into your codex. There are 12 to discover.

Hidden Assault is a hybrid of top-down strategy and stealth-action shooter. The game focuses on the pivotal role of modern technology, espionage, and sabotage in contemporary military tactics. In this world, the player is not the "center of the universe," but one of many participants in an active military conflict. Your objective is to support an AI-controlled allied army in defeating the enemy. To achieve this, your squad must carry out specialized missions, sabotage operations, assault actions, and more.

Global Map and Logistics

The Global Map represents the strategic heart of the game. It features settlements controlled by AI-driven allied forces or occupied by the enemy. These settlements autonomously form squads for defense, logistics, and assault operations. The liberation of captured settlements occurs independently of the player, led by specialized AI commanders.

Settlements utilize resources-such as food, water, and other supplies-to mobilize squads. If a settlement lacks the necessary resources to form a unit, it will be left defenseless. Settlements can exchange resources through logistical squads and supply chains. By intercepting enemy logistics and successfully completing missions, the player can deal a devastating blow to the opponent's overall military potential.

Action Missions

I have put extensive effort into making AI enemies truly dangerous-they utilize cover, deploy grenades, and employ tactical navigation to provide a serious challenge, especially for solo players. Typically, you operate as part of a squad of AI teammates whose primary role is to provide maximum support during combat and assist during stealth operations.

I have developed a Command Mode that allows for flexible squad management in the heat of battle, featuring a Command Delay function. This feature is particularly vital for stealth missions, as it allows you to coordinate and eliminate multiple targets simultaneously. Missions are initiated via the global map, where your squad can intervene in ongoing battles between allied and enemy forces to tip the scales of war.

Stealth Missions

The concepts of stealth and the "fog of war" apply to both the strategic global map and individual missions. On the global map, your squad can utilize the terrain for concealed movement. However, should an enemy patrol detect your presence, a battle will be initiated.

The foundation of espionage and sabotage operations lies in the Infiltration mechanic. Successfully embedding an operative into a location grants access to vital intelligence and opens up specialized sabotage missions.

Loadout Customization

Customize your loadout with a wide array of authentic weaponry, tactical gear, and cutting-edge technology. From silenced pistols and assault rifles to advanced drones and combat robots, your arsenal is your greatest asset.

Tactics and Сharacter Skill Development

Command specialized NPC partners, each with unique skills and expertise. Direct your squad's actions, utilizing their strengths to overcome any challenge. Gain experience by completing missions. Unlock more powerful character abilities.

Venture across an ever-changing map, choosing your path between battles, elite encounters, events, shops, and bonfires. Playing Cards, Reinvented

Build Rage. Unleash Hiss.

Keep playing cards to build Rage, then unleash Hiss when the moment is right. Combine different Talents and Enchantments to transform every Hiss into a devastating finishing blow.

Create Your Own Build

Experiment with 55+ Talents and a wide variety of Card Face Enchantments to forge your own playstyle. Even with the same deck of cards, every run can evolve into a completely different combat experience.

Every Adventure Is Unpredictable

Explore procedurally generated maps, balance risk and reward between events, shops, and bonfires, battle enemies and bosses with unique mechanics, and carve your own path through every adventure.

Dark Fantasy with a Touch of Black Humor

A world that is dangerous, mysterious, and delightfully absurd. Journey through a dark fantasy realm inhabited by animalfolk, where every adventure is filled with unexpected encounters, bizarre characters, and just enough black humor to keep you smiling.

Hist Maker: ReMake is a world history you can play. Each era is a level. You hold its people, events, objects and institutions, and you combine them two at a time to make what happened next: put Caesar and Legion together and you get the Gallic wars. Keep going, and you rebuild the era from the ground up.

69 eras, from antiquity to the early 20th century

East Asia, Europe, West Asia, Africa, South Asia and the Americas each run along their own timeline, and every era on it is a level with its own people and events. In Rome, slaves and gladiators rise with Spartacus. The Renaissance, the French Revolution and the Industrial Revolution are all here, and so are China's Three Kingdoms, where the Sun-Liu alliance meets Cao Cao at Red Cliffs, and Japan from the Sengoku warlords to the Meiji Restoration.

Put history together yourself

Each level's achievements name what you need to restore. In the French Revolution, "The republic tries a king" asks for the Republic, the Execution of Louis XVI and the Guillotine. Which two things lead to each is yours to work out from the history, and every step you figure out gives you one more element to use.

Restore the era's panorama

A panorama of the era runs along the bottom of the screen, and each achievement paints in more of it. In the Industrial Revolution, one river valley goes from a village with a sailing barge to water mills and pumping engines, then railways, factory halls, electric street lights at night, and finally a motor car on the road.

Every quotation has a source

Each combination comes with a one-line explanation, and about 6,000 quotations from historical sources appear as you discover things, each with its source. Combine Emperor Napoleon and Britain, and Trafalgar arrives with Nelson's signal: "England expects that every man will do his duty."

Help when you're stuck

An in-game assistant watches your deductions. If you keep circling the same elements, it speaks up: this element has nothing new to give with what you've found so far, or you still have new elements you haven't tried. It only points a direction; it never makes the combination for you.

For an easier time, spend the Restore Points you earn in play (not real money) at the assist shop: dim pairs that already failed, dim elements that can't lead anywhere, record formulas with a similar meaning automatically. Every assist can be switched on or off at any time, so you can turn them off when you'd rather work it out alone.

A remake of an eight-year-old game

The original Hist Maker came out free on Steam in 2018 with 8 levels and a rough interface. This version redraws the interface and the panoramas and grows the game to 69 levels. You don't need to have played the original.

Mods: edit levels, make your own

The game supports mods. Edit existing levels, or build new ones and add them to the level map, with your own elements, formulas and art. They don't have to be about history: a novel, a field of study or a world you made up all work. Publish to the Steam Workshop from inside the game, and play community levels other people have made. Mods use a separate save, so your main progress stays untouched.

What's inside

  • 69 eras across six regions
  • 3,400+ elements and 7,000+ combinations, each with an explanation
  • About 6,000 sourced quotations
  • 2,465 in-level achievements that restore each era's panorama
  • Adaptive hints, plus assists bought with in-game points and switchable at any time
  • Mod support: edit and create levels, Steam Workshop
  • English, Japanese and Simplified Chinese

A station you were never told about

An envelope, a set of keys, and the deed to a railway station no one in your family ever spoke of. You go to see what you have been left — and find that its platforms do not lead where platforms lead.

Four cities, a century apart

Each platform opens onto a real place at a real time: Berlin, Paris, New York, Hong Kong, decades apart. You are not shown a museum of them. You walk their streets, read their signs, speak to the people standing on their corners, and pick up what they left lying around.

A clue in one era changes another

This is the whole game. Something you read in one city means nothing until a thing you find in another tells you what it was. The notebook you carry between them is the only place those two halves ever meet — and the story is what you assemble in it, not what you are told.

Quiet, first-person, unhurried

No combat, no timers, no fail state. Historiker is about looking closely and following a thread across a hundred years, at your own pace.

A strategic roguelike about building bee colonies. Spend daylight gathering honey and growing the hive, then hold the line when hostile insects raid after dark.

  • Hatch specialised bees: workers, soldiers, gardeners, and nurses.

  • Found hives across 10 distinct biomes with unique hazards and native predators.

  • Adapt and optimise with 60 talents and 32 rewards.

  • Survive raids from 30 enemy types and 10 elites.

  • Claim victory with the Queen Rite, and push yourself to the limit with endless mode.

Colony Automation

Your bees have their own behavior and goals. Workers seek out flowers and gather honey, gardeners tend to flowers to keep them blooming, and nurses patch up the wounded and cure the sick. When invaders attack, your soldiers intercept them and fight to defend the hive. As Hivekeeper, your role is deciding which castes to hatch, which talents to unlock, and what rewards augment your build best.

Roguelike Rewards

After fighting off a raid or defeating a powerful elite, you are rewarded with a choice of 3 unique augments from a pool of 32.

The Talent Comb

Hive upgrades run through a hexagonal board of 60 talents. Unlock them all to gain access to the Queen Rite. The board layout partially randomises for each hive, keeping each run fresh and testing your ability to adapt.

Day and Night Cycles

During the day, worker and gardener bees busily make sure there is an incoming flow of honey. When the sun sets, raids begin. Enemy swarms move toward the hive from map edges or burst through underground tunnels. If defenders fall and invaders breach the core, the colony collapses. Surviving a night grants a choice of three randomised tactical rewards.

Every planet has a market. Every market has a customs officer.

Hold My Cargo is a first-person smuggling sim. Play it solo today; online co-op for up to four players is the first major Early Access update. You run a small trade ship between five planets, buy goods where they're cheap and sell them where they're not. The legal stuff pays the fuel. The illegal stuff pays for the ship.

Carry it yourself


No spreadsheets. Every crate is a real box you pick up, haul across the landing pad and drop into your hold. Contraband goes into the stashes — behind the cooling unit, under the cockpit floor, in the crew quarters — and it's your job to make sure nothing is sticking out when the customs officer walks up the ramp.

Talk your way through inspection

Customs officers come in flavours: by-the-book, corrupt, vengeful, bored. Fill in your declaration, decide what to admit to, and read the man in front of you. Bribe him, bluff him, or trust your stashes. In STANDARD every bust adds a WANTED star; in IRONMAN the third bust ends your career.

Co-op is next

Online co-op is not in the game yet — it's the first major Early Access update. When it lands, one of you distracts the officer at the terminal while the others quietly move the crates he shouldn't find. Or split up on the planet: one hits the trade office, one works the black market, one checks the tavern for rumours about tomorrow's prices.

Grow your operation

  • Three hulls to earn your way through: the starter SPAWN, the mid-size CRANK and the two-deck BELL with a full cargo bay and nine stashes.
  • Ship modules: deck guns against pirates, a cruise booster, a cold store for perishable goods, stash shielding against scanners, an escape shuttle.
  • Living cargo that spoils, pirates who take your marked crates if you can't pay, and a heat meter that remembers what you did last time.

Escape the galaxy. Then find out it wasn't the end.

Hit the target and jump off the Empire's map. The next galaxy has new planets, new residents, harsher laws and a bigger number to chase. You keep your ship, your modules and your reputation — the galaxy doesn't.

Made by a small crew

Hold My Cargo is developed by Favera Studio, a three-person team. It's a game about the gap between what you declared and what's actually in the hold. We hope you enjoy standing in it.
